pages.title: Maximum demand and diversity
pages.for: The largest current the installation, or one board, draws at any one time. You size the supply and every submain from it. Under Regulation 311.1 the designer assesses it.
pages.rule:
Lighting: I = W ÷ (230 × pf), fluorescent tube W × 1.25 first if no ballast loss is given
Neutral, same pf, no harmonics: IN = √(I1² + I2² + I3² − I1·I2 − I2·I3 − I3·I1)
Per phase, shared evenly: single-phase total after diversity ÷ 3, + each three-phase line current

Share single-phase circuits about equally over L1, L2 and L3. The heaviest phase sets the size.
Diversity figures are guidance, not a rule. Use them only where common sense allows.
EV points without load management: take no diversity. Some argue otherwise.

traps.text: Diversity treated as a rule. It is guidance and need not be applied.
Every single-phase circuit on one phase. The neutral then carries the lot.
traps.cite: Slides p.33; IET EngX forum, in research (unbalanced currents do not cancel)

traps.text: Fluorescent tube watts alone. The ballast's loss is extra.
traps.cite: Schneider Electrical Installation Guide, fluorescent lamps, in research

traps.text: The motor's line current divided by three with the single-phase loads. It is already a line current.
traps.cite: Slides p.13 (Ib of a three-phase load is a line current)

traps.text: Diversity on EV charge points without load management. Take none, though some argue for it.
traps.cite: The IEC wording in the Schneider guide (factor 1 without load management); BS 7671 722.311.201 (NAPIT) is the regulation that lets load curtailment count; argued on the IET EngX forum, in research

pages.task: There is a diversity percentage for lighting circuits. Is diversity a rule you must apply?
pages.answer: No: it is guidance, used where common sense allows
pages.why: The percentages come only from the On-Site Guide. So they are guidance, and you do not have to apply them.
pages.alt: The percentages come only from the On-Site Guide, so they are guidance. Ten 100 W lamps could be designed at 660 W rather than 1000 W. "BS 7671 sets them": it has no diversity table. The On-Site Guide gives the recognised figures. "Wherever the On-Site Guide gives one": you may still leave its figures off, such as 66% for domestic lighting or 90% for a shop's lighting.
options: No: it is guidance, used where common sense allows
Yes, wherever the On-Site Guide gives a percentage
pages.html:
The percentages come only from the On-Site Guide, so they are guidance. Ten 100 W lamps could be designed at 660 W rather than 1000 W.

"BS 7671 sets them": it has no diversity table. The On-Site Guide gives the recognised figures.

"Wherever the On-Site Guide gives one": you may still leave its figures off, such as 66% for domestic lighting or 90% for a shop's lighting.

pages.name: What it is for
pages.text: [[Maximum demand]] is the largest current an installation draws at any one time. You size the supply and each submain from it. Regulation 311.1 lets you work it out for the whole installation or for one part, so each board gets its own figure. Question 10 of the assignment asks for it. You may make informed assumptions where you need to. It links to question 1b, on balancing the loads.
pages.alt: If it is skipped or wrong: Too low, and the supply fuse or a submain's device and cable carries more than it was chosen for. Too high, and the cables are bigger and dearer than they need be. A figure with diversity is an estimate, and it may occasionally be exceeded.
pages.html:
If it is skipped or wrong: Too low, and the supply fuse or a submain's device and cable carries more than it was chosen for. Too high, and the cables are bigger and dearer than they need be.

pages.name: The why
pages.text: Put all seven of DBL2's lighting circuits on L1, and the neutral carries 24.35 A, as much as L1. Share them out over the three phases, and it carries just 0.30 A, harmonics aside. The heaviest phase is then 8.22 A.
pages.alt: Current in each conductor, on one scale L1 8.22 A L2 8.21 A L3 7.92 A Neutral 0.30 A L1 C1 4.89 A Consultation C5 3.33 A Showroom E L2 C3 5.71 A Toilets E and tea C6 2.50 A Reception L3 C2 4.08 A Toilets W C4 2.63 A Stores C7 1.21 A Foyer The phases carry 8.22 A on L1, 8.21 A on L2 and 7.92 A on L3. They are nearly equal, so they all but cancel. The neutral carries only 0.30 A, harmonics aside.

The phases carry 8.22 A on L1, 8.21 A on L2 and 7.92 A on L3. They are nearly equal, so they all but cancel. The neutral carries only 0.30 A, harmonics aside.

The neutral, for currents at about the same power factor

IN = √(I1² + I2² + I3² − I1·I2 − I2·I3 − I3·I1)

I1, I2 and I3 are the L1, L2 and L3 bars, and IN is the neutral bar. The rule adds three currents that are a third of a cycle apart.

It holds for mains-frequency currents only. Fluorescent and LED fittings also draw third-harmonic currents, which add in the neutral instead of cancelling. Lesson 4 covers those.

The card currents use practice values for ballast loss and power factor, from step 6.

pages.name: Check
pages.task: A board's lighting circuits carry 10 A on L1, 10 A on L2 and 4 A on L3, at about the same power factor. What does the neutral carry?
pages.why: The 4 A on each phase cancels. That leaves 6 A on L1 and 6 A on L2, a third of a cycle apart, and those add to 6 A. By the rule: √(100 + 100 + 16 − 100 − 40 − 40) = √36 = 6.00 A.
pages.html: √(100 + 100 + 16 − 100 − 40 − 40) = √36 = 6.00 A

pages.name: Diversity
pages.text: Not every load runs flat out at once, so a building draws less than its connected load. [[Diversity]] means designing with common sense rather than for the maximum.
pages.alt: These are the On-Site Guide's allowances for small shops, stores, offices and business premises. We treat the showroom as one of those. Commercial work may need measured loads instead. Lighting: 90% of the total current demand Heating and power: 100% of the largest appliance + 75% of the rest Motors: 100% of the largest + 80% of the second largest + 60% of the rest (the showroom has only one) Standard circuits: 100% of the largest circuit + 50% of every other Only these four are used here. The rest are in Appendix A.
pages.html:
These are the On-Site Guide's allowances for small shops, stores, offices and business premises. We treat the showroom as one of those. Commercial work may need measured loads instead.

  • Lighting: 90% of the total current demand
  • Heating and power: 100% of the largest appliance + 75% of the rest
  • Motors: 100% of the largest + 80% of the second largest + 60% of the rest (the showroom has only one)
  • Standard circuits: 100% of the largest circuit + 50% of every other

Only these four are used here. The rest are in Appendix A.

EV charge points: allow no diversity, a factor of 1, unless a load management system controls them. Regulation 722.311 lets load curtailment count. On this job, load management is optional.

Where it's argued
  • Some say BS 7671 does not forbid diversity on EV points. Others say that without load management you still allow none.
  • Some apply 66% to a single lighting circuit's Ib. Others apply diversity only to the total at the origin. Another view is that it is only rarely right for one circuit.
  • Another method applies a factor to the loads on each board. Where they are mainly lighting, it advises a factor close to 1.

What we assume: all the lighting at 100%. Question 5a has the internal showroom lights on from 7.30 am to 9 pm, and we take the rest of the lighting with them. The On-Site Guide would allow 90%. That is a designer's call.

Practice values: 25%, 0.96 and 0.95. The drawing does not name the fittings' gear. On a real job, use the maker's figures. A separate driver's watts are extra.

An older method takes lamp watts × 1.8 ÷ voltage for discharge lighting, at a power factor of at least 0.85. We use the first method here.

DBL2's share, as we split the building

DBL2 sits in the tools and warranty store and feeds the east of the building. That is the consultation bay, the toilets, cleaner and tea bay, the two stores, the showroom east of the welcome desk, service reception, the foyer and the walkway bollards. DBL1 feeds the rest.

Counted on the lighting drawing: 55 LED 26 W, 18 modular 4 × 36 W, 4 twin 58 W and 6 walkway bollards 18 W.

The key does not say whether a twin's 58 W is each tube or the whole fitting. We take two 58 W tubes, 116 W, the cautious reading.

55 × 26 = 1430 W; 18 × 144 = 2592 W; 4 × 116 = 464 W; 6 × 18 = 108 W; 1430 + 2592 + 464 + 108 = 4594 W

pages.task: Take the showroom's lighting at 100%, eight 32 A socket circuits as standard circuits, the fixed points as heating and power, four 32 A EV outlets with no diversity, and the motor's 23.08 A. (c) Determine the maximum demand of the installation, per phase.

DBL2: 8.22 + 8.21 + 7.92 = 24.35 A. DBL1: 38.74 A, worked the same way from its 103 LED, 16 modular, 12 twin and 6 bulkheads. The bulkheads go with the LEDs: watts ÷ (230 × 0.95), with no ballast allowance. DBL1's 9 wall spots (2 × 35 W) and 6 columns (70 W) are taken at a power factor of 0.9. That is a practice value with no source, as the lamps are not named.
pages.html:
Carried forward
(a)Motor's design current, Ib23.08 A
(b)DBL2's lighting: current on L18.22 A
Given, each practice value marked

Lighting, at 100%: question 5a has the showroom lights on from 7.30 am to 9 pm. DBL2: 8.22 + 8.21 + 7.92 = 24.35 A. DBL1: 38.74 A, worked the same way from its 103 LED, 16 modular, 12 twin and 6 bulkheads. The bulkheads go with the LEDs: watts ÷ (230 × 0.95), with no ballast allowance. DBL1's 9 wall spots (2 × 35 W) and 6 columns (70 W) are taken at a power factor of 0.9. That is a practice value with no source, as the lamps are not named.

Sockets: eight 32 A circuits, one per area. Each is taken at its rating, a practice value. Treat them as standard circuits: 100% of the largest + 50% of every other.

Fixed points: three 20 A DP switches and a 32 A rotary isolator. Each is taken at its rating, a practice value. Treat them as heating and power: 100% of the largest + 75% of the rest.

EV charging: two charging points, each with two 32 A outlets. Take them as four single-phase outlets with no diversity. That is a practice value, as the drawing does not say whether the outlets are single- or three-phase. The 63 A TPN isolators are not part of the circuit.

The motor: at 100%, as it is the only one. Its line current from 1(a) goes on every phase.

Sharing: the single-phase loads are shared evenly over the three phases, so divide their total by 3.

Lighting: 24.35 + 38.74 = 63.09 A

Sockets: 32 + 0.5 × 7 × 32 = 32 + 112 = 144.00 A

Fixed points: 32 + 0.75 × 3 × 20 = 32 + 45 = 77.00 A

EV: 4 × 32 = 128.00 A

63.09 + 144.00 + 77.00 + 128.00 = 412.09 A; 412.09 ÷ 3 = 137.36 A; 137.36 + 23.08 = 160.44 A

About 160 A a phase. It is an estimate on practice values, which question 10 allows.

A real split is heavier on one phase. Four 32 A EV outlets cannot share evenly over three phases, so one phase carries two: 2 × 32 = 64 A. An even share would be 128 ÷ 3 = 42.67 A. That phase stays heavier unless other circuits move off it.

A Section A style question, worked on the showroom drawings.

pages.name: Section B
pages.task: State two reasons a designer applies diversity.
pages.why: A model answer: Not every load runs at full current at the same time. So designing for every load at once overstates what the installation draws. Diversity means designing with common sense rather than for the maximum. It keeps cable sizes smaller and costs lower. It also lets you choose the supply, submains and switchgear for the demand they will really carry. The figures come from the On-Site Guide. They are guidance, used with judgement, not a rule.
